completeSourceDiscovery.boundaryContinuationRule: a move beginning in lookbehind remains owned by the predecessor chunk

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: The universe began to exist and therefore has a transcendent, timeless, immaterial, personal cause.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Craig at the podium, and the uninterrupted opening address remains his until the next speaker transition.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This cosmological argument is the first of Craig's three expressly cumulative reasons for affirming the existence of God.
candidates.contextSummary: Craig combines philosophical objections to an actually infinite past with scientific claims about a past boundary, then infers a personal transcendent creator.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Objective moral values and duties exist, require God as their foundation, and therefore support God's existence.
candidates.attributionBasis: This numbered argument occurs within Craig's uninterrupted opening address after his cosmological case and before his historical case.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument supplies the moral character absent from the cosmological conclusion and forms a distinct pillar of Craig's cumulative case.
candidates.contextSummary: Craig argues that naturalistic evolution cannot make morality objectively binding, affirms objective moral experience, and infers God as its necessary ground.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: The empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and disciples' belief are best explained by Jesus's resurrection, supporting the Christian God.
candidates.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly introduces his third numbered argument and develops it continuously until beginning the summary of his opening case.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This historical argument moves Craig's case from generic monotheism to the specifically Christian conception of God identified in the motion.
candidates.contextSummary: Craig presents three historical claims about Jesus, rejects naturalistic explanations as implausible, and treats resurrection as the best explanation.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Law
candidates.proposition: The immense scale and depth of apparently gratuitous animal and human suffering provide powerful evidence against an omnipotent, omniscient, good God.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Law, who announces one opening argument and develops the evidential problem of evil throughout this uninterrupted passage.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is Law's expressly selected argument against God's existence and the principal evidential challenge that Craig must answer in the debate.
candidates.contextSummary: Law surveys prolonged animal suffering and pervasive child mortality, arguing that a perfectly good and powerful deity would need adequate reasons for every instance.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Law
candidates.proposition: Good-God belief faces a symmetry challenge because observed evil undermines it just as observed good undermines an otherwise parallel evil-God hypothesis.
candidates.attributionBasis: Law remains the sole speaker and explicitly pivots from his evidential argument to an alternative evil-creator hypothesis and its mirrored problem.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The evil-God symmetry is the debate's defining challenge and directly tests whether Craig can justify treating good and evil creator hypotheses differently.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's opening case for a good creator, especially the moral neutrality of his cosmological conclusion.

candidates.contextSummary: Law argues that Craig's cosmological reasoning does not identify the creator's moral character, then parallels the problems of evil and good.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Law
candidates.proposition: Standard explanations of evil can largely be mirrored to explain good under an evil God, so those defenses do not break the symmetry.
candidates.attributionBasis: Law continuously develops mirrored versions of familiar theodicies within his opening turn, with no intervening change of speaker or topic ownership.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The reversibility claim supports the symmetry challenge by arguing that free will, natural laws, soul-making, mystery, and compensation work equally both ways.
candidates.contextSummary: Law reverses free-will, law-governed-world, soul-making, mysterious-reasons, and afterlife defenses to construct corresponding defenses of an evil deity.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Law
candidates.proposition: If observation can make an evil God highly unlikely despite mirrored defenses, it should likewise make a good God highly unlikely unless a major asymmetry is shown.
candidates.attributionBasis: Law concludes his opening case in a continuous passage explicitly framing the challenge he is placing before Craig for the ensuing response.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This passage states the ultimate comparative burden of Law's challenge and applies it directly to Craig's arguments and anticipated skeptical defense.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's cumulative arguments for a good God and any appeal to unknown divine reasons for observed suffering.

candidates.contextSummary: Law maintains that mystery cannot privilege good-God belief because it also protects evil-God belief, and asks Craig to establish a significant evidential difference.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: The evidential problem of evil fails unless the atheist can show that God probably lacks morally sufficient reasons and that a better feasible world exists.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Craig's first response, and Craig directly identifies Law's evidential problem before presenting this uninterrupted initial rebuttal.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is Craig's first substantive answer to Law's sole opening argument and shifts the burden toward demonstrating feasible alternatives with less suffering.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Law's claim that the quantity and intensity of apparently gratuitous suffering make a perfectly good God highly unlikely.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig distinguishes emotional force from philosophical proof, proposes that suffering may facilitate freely knowing God, and demands a feasible superior world.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: The observed suffering does not establish God's nonexistence because atheists cannot show that God probably lacks morally sufficient reasons for permitting it.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Craig's response, and the uninterrupted first-person rebuttal continues under his identified turn.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly contests Law's evidential problem of evil by assigning the crucial burden to claims about God's possible reasons and feasible worlds.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Law's evidential inference from extensive suffering to the probable nonexistence of a good God.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig distinguishes the emotional force of suffering from its philosophical force and invokes salvation-related purposes that may require a suffering-permitting feasible world.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: The evil-God symmetry does not undermine traditional theism because divine goodness is not inferred inductively from worldly goods, while an evil creator would not literally be God.
candidates.attributionBasis: This is a continuous portion of Craig's explicitly introduced rebuttal, with first-person references to his own argument.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move directly answers the debate's defining evil-God challenge by disputing both its terminology and its assumed inductive basis for divine goodness.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Law's claim that worldly evil defeats a good God just as worldly good defeats an evil God.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig separates an evil creator from a worship-worthy God, accepts parity between simple inductive arguments, and grounds theistic belief in goodness through a moral argument instead.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: The reality of evil supports God's existence because objective moral values exist and would lack a foundation if God did not exist.
candidates.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly announces a final point, states the premises and conclusion, and summarizes it within his uninterrupted speaking turn.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This converts the central evidence invoked against theism into an affirmative moral argument for God and supplies a principal component of Craig's cumulative case.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Law's use of evil and suffering as affirmative evidence against the existence of the good God of traditional theism.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig presents a compact moral syllogism, invokes Law's prior acknowledgment that such an argument might be promising, and includes it in his three-part summary.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Law
candidates.proposition: The evidential problem can be framed solely in terms of excessive suffering, so it neither presupposes objective evil nor depends on moral realism.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Law's rebuttal, and Law explicitly identifies and answers Craig's claim that evil proves God.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This blocks Craig's attempt to turn the problem of evil into a moral argument by showing that Law's evidential challenge can avoid moral predicates entirely.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's contention that recognizing evil presupposes objective moral values and therefore supports God's existence.

candidates.contextSummary: Law argues that even a moral nihilist can observe an enormous and apparently purposeless quantity of suffering, leaving the evidential objection intact without the concept of evil.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Law
candidates.proposition: If observation warrants confident rejection of an omnipotent evil God because of abundant good, it likewise warrants rejecting an omnipotent good God because of abundant suffering.
candidates.attributionBasis: Law explicitly marks this as Craig's other main argument and develops the symmetry challenge continuously through the end of the point.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the core evil-God symmetry challenge: it claims that Craig's skeptical response imposes an implausible double standard between parallel deity hypotheses.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's concession that worldly goods do not disprove an evil creator and his appeal to unknown divine purposes.

candidates.contextSummary: Law says ordinary empirical observation makes an evil deity unreasonable beyond reasonable doubt and argues that the sheer quantity of suffering should permit the parallel judgment about a good deity.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Law has not answered Craig's cosmological, moral, or resurrection arguments, and the cosmological argument still establishes a personal creator even without establishing that creator's goodness.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator returns Craig to the podium, after which Craig inventories his three previously presented arguments in an uninterrupted response.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move reasserts Craig's cumulative affirmative case and argues that the problem of evil cannot defeat a cosmological conclusion that does not specify the creator's moral character.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Law's rebuttal concentrating on the evil-God challenge and evidential suffering rather than Craig's cumulative affirmative arguments.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig maintains that Law must engage the origin argument, defends objective morality as more certain than skepticism, and notes that the resurrection case has not yet been addressed.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Law's symmetry does not show that a good God lacks sufficient reasons, because the purposes of any universe-making being may predictably exceed human discernment and divine goodness is not inferred from worldly appearances.
candidates.attributionBasis: Craig announces numbered responses to Law's atheistic argument and develops the first two points continuously in his identified rebuttal.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly answers the evil-God symmetry by accepting limited inductive parity while denying that either inscrutable goods or evils strongly determine a creator's moral character.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Law's argument that empirical rejection of an evil God licenses parallel empirical rejection of a good God.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig says Law has not established the absence of morally sufficient reasons, agrees that goods alone do not disprove an evil creator, and emphasizes the world's moral ambiguity.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Avoiding the moral argument by describing only pain and suffering requires abandoning objective moral values, whose objectivity atheism leaves unexplained.
candidates.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly introduces his third response and directly addresses Law's proposal to formulate the argument without moral evil.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move defends Craig's moral argument against Law's reframing by contending that affirmation of objective morality restores the need for a theistic explanation.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Law's contention that the evidential problem needs only suffering and can be advanced without affirming objective evil.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig accepts that suffering can be discussed without moral terminology but argues that Law then faces a choice between moral antirealism and an unresolved account of objective values and duties.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Law
candidates.proposition: Craig has not justified either premise of the moral argument, and when that argument is combined with the evidential problem of evil it may support moral skepticism rather than theism.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Law's next rebuttal, and Law explicitly turns to Craig's arguments before sustaining a detailed critique of the moral argument.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This challenges a principal affirmative argument for God at both premises and denies that intuitive confidence in objective values can outweigh the counterevidence from suffering.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's claim that objective moral values exist, require God as their foundation, and are more evident than moral skepticism.

candidates.contextSummary: Law cites philosophical disagreement, argues that rejecting one evolutionary account does not exclude every atheist-friendly account, and says strong contrary evidence can overturn an initially compelling moral intuition.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Law
candidates.proposition: Reports surrounding Jesus's resurrection provide little evidential support for a miracle because baffling testimony is expected to arise occasionally even when no miracle occurs.
candidates.attributionBasis: Law explicitly turns to the resurrection argument and carries the resulting analogy and evidential conclusion through the delivered lookahead.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly engages Craig's previously unanswered resurrection argument by challenging the claimed explanatory force of testimony, multiple attestation, and apparent corroboration.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's argument that the empty tomb and post-crucifixion appearances are best explained by Jesus's divine resurrection.

candidates.contextSummary: Law uses a well-attested but mistaken UFO report to illustrate that impressive eyewitness and corroborative details can accompany mundane events, then applies that base-rate point to biblical reports.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: The unrefuted cosmological argument establishes an immaterial, uncaused, timeless, spaceless, enormously powerful personal creator of the universe.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Craig, and the uninterrupted first-person summation explicitly restates his opening cosmological argument.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies the creator component of Craig's cumulative case and directly bears on whether any divine creator exists.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Law's decision not to engage Craig's cosmological argument during the principal exchange.

candidates.contextSummary: In his closing summation, Craig contends that Law left the universe's origin argument unanswered and states the attributes he thinks follow from it.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Atheism lacks an adequate explanation for objective moral values and duties, whereas God's nature and commands provide their transcendent foundation.
candidates.attributionBasis: Craig continues his announced summation, addresses Law by name, and restates the premises and explanatory rationale of his moral argument.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The moral argument is Craig's principal means of moving from a morally neutral creator toward a good God in his cumulative case.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Law's criticism that Craig had not justified the moral argument's first premise and his reference to dissenting philosophers.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig answers Law's appeal to philosophical disagreement by citing atheists who accept the premise and arguing that naturalism cannot ground an objective moral realm.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Jesus's resurrection best satisfies standard explanatory criteria and gains special plausibility from Jesus's life, ministry, and divine claims.
candidates.attributionBasis: The same uninterrupted Craig summation explicitly turns to the resurrection and contrasts his explanation with Law's paranormal-report analogy.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The resurrection argument is Craig's specifically Christian evidence and therefore bears directly on the motion's Christian-theism conclusion.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Law's argument that baffling miracle reports predictably arise without miracles and therefore provide little evidential support.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig accepts that paranormal reports warrant caution but argues that the resurrection has superior explanatory performance and a relevant religious-historical context.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Observed evil does not disprove a good creator because humans cannot confidently judge that God lacks morally sufficient reasons for permitting particular suffering.
candidates.attributionBasis: Craig's closing statement explicitly identifies Law's evil-God objection and gives his final symmetry and skeptical-theist response to it.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly answers the debate's central evidential problem of evil and evil-God symmetry challenge to Christian theism.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Law's evil-God symmetry challenge and claim that extensive suffering is strong observational evidence against a good God.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig argues that goods cannot alone disprove an evil creator and evils cannot alone disprove a good creator, because relevant divine reasons may exceed human judgment.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Law
candidates.proposition: The immense historical scale of sentient suffering is powerful observational evidence against Craig's good God, and Craig's skeptical replies work equally for an evil God.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Law's summation, after which Law recapitulates his suffering evidence, evil-God comparison, and criticism of Craig's mystery defense.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This states Law's principal evidential case against the motion and the core symmetry test Craig's cumulative case must overcome.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's claim that unknown morally sufficient divine reasons prevent observed suffering from counting decisively against a good God.

candidates.contextSummary: Law emphasizes suffering across sentient history, says Craig mostly invoked unknowable reasons, and argues those same defenses leave good-God belief no better supported than evil-God belief.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Law
candidates.proposition: Craig's moral argument has an unjustified first premise and cannot counterbalance evil because, combined with the suffering evidence, it may instead imply moral nihilism.
candidates.attributionBasis: Law's uninterrupted closing summation explicitly isolates Craig's moral argument, states its first premise, and explains the alleged dialectical circularity.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This attacks Craig's main argument for the creator's goodness and denies that it can offset the evidential problem of evil.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's contention that objective moral values require God and that this moral argument contributes goodness to his cumulative case.

candidates.contextSummary: Law says Craig never established that objective morality requires God and argues that using the premise against suffering presupposes that the evidential problem has already been resolved.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Law
candidates.proposition: Bracketing the cosmological argument does not concede a creator, and that argument supplies no grounds for preferring an all-good creator over an all-evil one.
candidates.attributionBasis: A moderator question cues Law, who explicitly denies Craig's characterization of his position and explains the restricted scope of his debate strategy.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This clarifies the symmetry challenge's scope and denies that Craig's cosmological component contributes support for the specifically good God at issue.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's accusation that Law effectively conceded a creator by declining to answer the cosmological argument.

candidates.contextSummary: Law distinguishes a neutral creator from Craig's God, denies conceding either, and says origin arguments are silent about whether a creator is morally good or evil.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Law
candidates.proposition: Craig's cumulative case could support an evil God equally well, while his moral argument remains too weak to outweigh the observational evidence against either extreme deity.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator requests Law's response to the moral argument, and Law directly compares Craig's proposed cumulative cases for good and evil gods.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move integrates Law's symmetry challenge, evidential evil argument, and objection to the moral premise into a direct answer to Craig's cumulative case.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's explanation that cosmological, fine-tuning, moral, and resurrection arguments cumulatively build a theologically rich concept of God.

candidates.contextSummary: Law argues the morally neutral creator argument can enter either cumulative case and that even granting the moral premise alongside suffering may yield denial of objective morality.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Law
candidates.proposition: Craig bears the burden of ruling out atheist-friendly foundations for objective morality, and dismissing one evolutionary account does not establish that none are possible.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator asks for Law's objection, and Law directly identifies Craig's claim as unsupported while discussing alternative atheistic and nonnaturalistic possibilities.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This targets the inferential premise essential to Craig's moral argument and challenges whether his explanatory complaint supplies sufficient support.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's assertion that atheism has no explanatory basis for objective duties, obligations, prohibitions, or intrinsic human moral value.

candidates.contextSummary: Law says an assertion of explanatory deficiency is not enough, notes atheism need not entail naturalism, and argues Craig has not excluded the range of possible accounts.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: The cosmological argument deduces an uncaused, timeless, spaceless, immaterial, enormously powerful personal creator from what a cause of the universe must be.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator addresses Craig by name, and Craig corrects the question's formulation before restating his conclusion and defense of a cause of the universe.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This provides Craig's final clarification of the cosmological conclusion and extends the move into the delivered lookahead to its actual ending.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The audience question asking why ignorance about cosmic origins should lead to positing God rather than acknowledging limits to understanding.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig distinguishes his stated creator conclusion from an immediate conclusion to God and argues that a beginning cannot arise uncaused from nothing.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Law
candidates.proposition: Even a cogent cosmological argument would support an evil creator as much as a good God and therefore cannot establish Craig's God without further arguments.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly directs the cosmological question to Stephen, whose ensuing first-person answer contrasts Craig's God with an evil God.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This applies the evil-God symmetry challenge directly to Craig's cosmological argument and contests its contribution to the cumulative case.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's claim that the universe's beginning deductively entails a timeless, spaceless, powerful personal creator.

candidates.contextSummary: After Craig describes what follows from a cause of the universe, Law argues that those conclusions do not identify the creator's moral character and require supplementation.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Not knowing why the universe exists is insufficient because the cosmological conclusion follows deductively unless one rejects either the universe's beginning or its transcendent cause.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator asks whether Law's profession of ignorance is sufficient, and Craig answers in the first person while restating his deductive premises.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move defends the logical force of Craig's cosmological argument and rejects the characterization of it as an appeal to gaps in scientific knowledge.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Law's answer that he does not know why the universe exists and his refusal to engage first-cause reasoning.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig distinguishes a philosophical deduction from a God-of-the-gaps inference and says scientific evidence supports, but does not constitute, the premise that the universe began.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Law
candidates.proposition: Acknowledging ignorance about why the universe exists does not prevent rationally excluding some answers, including an evil God whose existence the observed world's goods strongly disconfirm.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator invites Stephen to respond, and the ensuing first-person remarks explicitly compare his ignorance with the rational rejection of an evil God.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies the epistemic principle underlying Law's evidential challenge: incomplete explanation is compatible with strong evidence against a specified divine hypothesis.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's contention that merely saying one does not know is inadequate unless a premise of the cosmological argument is denied.

candidates.contextSummary: Law distinguishes inability to answer an ultimate explanatory question from inability to rule out proposed answers, then uses observed goods to illustrate the distinction with evil-God belief.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Theists do not infer God's existence from an inductive inventory of worldly goods, so Law's observational comparison does not mirror the actual basis of Christian theism.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn directly disagrees with Stephen and invokes theistic philosophers and a publication associated with Law while defending how theists reason.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The objection challenges whether Law's evil-God comparison accurately tracks the inferential structure of Craig's cumulative theistic case.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Law's claim that the observed character of the world gives a powerful evidential case against an evil God.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig answers Law's appeal to observed goods by denying that Christian theists establish God's existence through a comparable inductive survey of the world's good features.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Law
candidates.proposition: The observational argument is not meant to establish a good or evil deity but to rule out a deity with a specified moral character when the world's features conflict with that character.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker immediately corrects Craig's description of the argument and restates in first-person terms what the observational inference is intended to establish.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This clarification preserves the core evidential symmetry by distinguishing evidence against a divine hypothesis from a positive inference to its moral opposite.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's objection that theists have never inferred God's existence from an inductive survey of worldly goods.

candidates.contextSummary: Law explains that worldly observations can exclude a deity of a certain character without proving the existence of the opposite deity, illustrating this with goods that count against evil God.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Human cognitive limitations prevent reliable probability judgments that apparently gratuitous goods or evils lack morally sufficient purposes within an omniscient being's providential plan.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker refers back to a point previously made from Stephen Wykstra and develops Craig's characteristic skeptical-theist response concerning divine purposes.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is Craig's principal rebuttal to Law's observational evidential inference and directly challenges the probability judgment needed by both problem-of-evil formulations.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Law's claim that observable love, laughter, and other goods allow rational exclusion of an evil God.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig argues that an omnipotent and omniscient being may pursue ends inaccessible to human observers, undermining inductive judgments from apparently gratuitous features of the world.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Law
candidates.proposition: The same appeal to inscrutable purposes can defend evil God, so skeptical mystery cannot defeat the observational case without an argument showing why humans cannot make the relevant judgment.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn explicitly applies Craig's skeptical strategy to evil-God belief and demands an argument rather than a bare assertion of unknowability.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the direct symmetry counterreply to skeptical theism and argues that Craig's defense has an unacceptable consequence for the acknowledged rejection of evil God.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's skeptical-theist claim that limited humans cannot judge whether apparent goods or evils serve unknown divine purposes.

candidates.contextSummary: Law argues that Craig's cognitive-limitation defense transfers unchanged to evil God, which people nevertheless reject, and insists that the alleged inability to judge requires independent support.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Historical consequences propagate beyond human epistemic reach, so people cannot know that a providential God lacks morally sufficient reasons for permitting a particular instance of suffering.
candidates.attributionBasis: The answer recalls Craig's earlier citation of James Clerk Maxwell and articulates a providential ripple-effect account of morally sufficient reasons for suffering.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move provides Craig's requested argument for skeptical theism by identifying long-range causal consequences that constrain judgments about apparently gratuitous suffering.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Law's demand for an actual argument establishing why humans cannot judge divine reasons from observed goods and evils.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig grounds human uncertainty in the extended ripple effects of historical events, whose morally relevant outcomes may arise far outside an observer's lifetime or location.

candidates.speaker: Stephen Law
candidates.proposition: Unexplained and apparently strong testimony arises predictably even for false extraordinary claims, so difficult-to-explain resurrection reports do not by themselves support the resurrection hypothesis.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Doctor Law to recap his fundamental objection, and the answer develops his earlier comparison with miracle, alien, and anomalous-object reports.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This attacks the resurrection component of Craig's cumulative case by denying that otherwise unexplained reports discriminate between the supernatural hypothesis and its falsity.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's argument that historical evidence for Jesus's resurrection supports God's existence within his cumulative case.

candidates.contextSummary: Law uses a well-attested anomalous sighting later attributable to Venus to argue that some impressive cases will remain hard to explain regardless of whether extraordinary hypotheses are true.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Jesus's resurrection was unexpected within the disciples' Judaism and messianic expectations, distinguishing it from desired paranormal reports and adding explanatory warrant to the event.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly requests one brief response from Bill, and the answer contrasts the resurrection with reports generated by an appetite for paranormal phenomena.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This defends the resurrection evidence by contesting Law's expectation premise and identifying an allegedly distinctive feature of the disciples' reported belief.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Law's contention that hard-to-explain extraordinary reports are expected even when the extraordinary hypothesis is false.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig argues that the disciples did not anticipate the resurrection because it conflicted with their inherited Jewish and messianic framework, reducing the force of Law's analogy.
